prisoner.name: Abraham Lincoln Woods Jr.
prisoner.description: Abraham Lincoln Woods Jr. was an Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights cofounder and a Birmingham civil rights minister. He led an early department-store sit-in and spent five days in jail during the 1963 campaign. He later led the Birmingham SCLC and taught at Miles College.
affiliation: Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights

cases.charges: Arrest following a Birmingham department-store desegregation sit-in; exact charge unresolved
cases.sentence: Spent five days in jail following the sit-in. Exact admission and release dates and any separate sentence remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: The HistoryMakers interview biography explicitly records five days jailed following his first department-store sit-in.
entries.research_notes: Congressional tribute places the first sit-in in spring 1963. No exact arrest day or statute inferred from the broader campaign chronology. Abraham is not his brother Calvin, who already has a profile.

prisoner.name: Charles Avery Jr.
prisoner.description: Charles Avery Jr. led fellow Hooper City High School students into the Birmingham Children's Crusade in May 1963. He spent five days in Birmingham Jail after marching against segregation and later continued local civil rights work.

cases.charges: Arrest during the Birmingham Children's Crusade; exact charge unresolved
cases.sentence: Reported spending five days in Birmingham Jail after the May 7, 1963 student march. Exact release date and any separate sentence remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: In his published interview Avery identifies the May 7 march and reports five days actually spent in Birmingham Jail.
entries.research_notes: Do not calculate a birth year from his reported age or a release date from inclusive day counts. Campaign participation is verified; formal ACMHR or SCLC membership is not assumed.

prisoner.name: Janice Wesley Kelsey
prisoner.description: Janice Wesley Kelsey joined the Birmingham Children's Crusade as an Ullman High School student. Arrested on May 2, 1963, she was held for four days. She later became an educator and wrote about her experience in the civil rights movement.

cases.charges: Parading without a permit, according to her account of the arresting officer's stated city-ordinance violation
cases.sentence: Held for four days after the May 2, 1963 march. Her oral history describes initial juvenile processing and a first night at the county jail. Exact release date and judicial disposition remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: NPR's interview report states four days held; her recorded oral history independently describes arrest and overnight confinement.
entries.research_notes: She says she had turned sixteen in April but told police fifteen. Neither an approximate age nor the deliberately inaccurate booking age is converted into a birthdate. Do not identify her with Cynthia Wesley.

prisoner.name: Freeman A. Hrabowski III
prisoner.description: Freeman A. Hrabowski III participated in the Birmingham Children's Crusade in May 1963. As a child protester he spent five days in juvenile detention. He later became a mathematics educator and president of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.

cases.charges: Arrest during the Birmingham Children's Crusade; exact charge unresolved
cases.sentence: His Civil Rights History Project interview records five days in juvenile detention in May 1963. Exact admission and release days and judicial disposition remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: The recorded interview explicitly states five days in juvenile confinement; his own 2013 article dates the episode to May 1963.
entries.research_notes: Do not substitute his father or grandfather with the same name. The oral history rejects the interviewer's fairgrounds suggestion; no unsupported institution link is assigned.

prisoner.name: Mamie King-Chalmers
prisoner.description: Mamie King-Chalmers organized neighbors to join Birmingham's 1963 civil rights demonstrations. She endured police violence and spent five days in jail. She later shared her experiences with students and through oral-history interviews.

cases.charges: Arrest during Birmingham desegregation protests; exact charge unresolved
cases.sentence: Her interview biography records five days in jail during the 1963 Birmingham campaign. Exact admission and release dates and any separate sentence remain unverified.

prisoner.aka: Mamie King Chalmers; Mamie Chalmers; Mamie King

entries.custody_evidence: Her participant-approved interview biography records a five-day jail stay.
entries.research_notes: Death date resolves the daughter's statement that she died Tuesday, reported by AP on Friday December 2, 2022, to November 29. No custody date is inferred from the separate May 3 firehose photograph.
